title: Movement-related changes in pain perception and the role of cue informativeness
summary:
Pain is more than just an unpleasant sensation – it prompts us to move in order to prevent or limit tissue damage. Pain and motor behavior are therefore closely linked: pain changes how we move, and conversely, movement can influence how intensely we perceive pain.

An earlier study by this research group looked into this. Healthy adults received brief electrical stimuli on a finger – sometimes painful, sometimes not. Sometimes they were allowed to move the finger away, and sometimes they were instructed to keep it still. The results revealed something surprising: when movement was allowed, painful stimuli were perceived as stronger and non-painful ones as weaker. It remains unclear why this is the case.

We suspect that expectations play an important role here. Our brain does not only process pain; it also constantly compares what it expects with what it actually feels. When we are allowed to move while in pain, it gives us a certain sense of control. This sense of control might sharpen our expectations to the point where we perceive painful stimuli as even more painful and non-painful stimuli as even more harmless.

In our study, we investigate whether this is actually the case. To do so, we vary how much participants know in advance: sometimes they are told exactly what to expect, and sometimes it remains open. In addition, after each individual stimulus we record how intensely it was perceived, allowing us to examine the relationship between movement and pain perception even more closely.
conditions: Mechanisms of pain processing in healthy participants

interventions.name: Healthy participants receive painful and non-painful electrotactile stimuli and are instructed either to withdraw their finger from the electrode upon stimulus perception, or to keep it on the electrode throughout the stimulation (within-subjects design).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Right-handedness
Exclusion criteria:
- Body mass index <18 or >30
- Presence of acute or chronic somatic or psychiatric illnesses (based on self-report or routine examination)
- Participation in other studies involving medication, or regular medication intake (except thyroid, allergy medication, occasional use of pain medication)
- Intake of pain medication within 24 hours prior to start of examination
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Acute skin disease or injury at the sites to be stimulated
